About the Fuggerei
The Fuggerei is the oldest social housing complex in the world still in use. It was founded in 1521 by the Augsburg merchant and banker Jakob Fugger “the Rich” as a settlement for citizens of Augsburg who had fallen into need through no fault of their own. Today it consists of 67 houses with 142 apartments, together with its own church and administrative buildings, enclosed by a wall with gates that are still locked at night.
Remarkably, the rent has never been raised in more than 500 years: residents pay one Rhenish guilder per year — today €0.88 — plus a daily commitment to three prayers for the founder and his family. Around 150 people live there under these conditions. Several small museums on the grounds document the founding of the settlement, everyday life in it today, and its destruction during the Second World War.


Getting there by tram
From the workshop venue: take tram line 3 towards Augsburg Hauptbahnhof from the stop Innovationspark/LfU (about a 3-minute walk east of Building W) to Königsplatz, then change to tram line 1 towards Lechhausen Neuer Ostfriedhof and get off at the stop Fuggerei. The main entrance is directly at the stop.
From the city centre or the main station: any tram or bus to Königsplatz, then line 1 towards Lechhausen Neuer Ostfriedhof to Fuggerei. The Fuggerei is also only a few minutes’ walk from the city centre.

title: SciML Frontiers: Progress, Evolution, and Future Directions — Workshop 2026
text:
22–23 September 2026 • Augsburg, Germany



Scientific Machine Learning (SciML), the fusion of scientific computing and machine learning algorithms, has proven to be a transformative force in academia and is rapidly establishing a firm foothold in industrial applications. A foundational 2018 workshop outlined six priority research directions (PRDs) for the nascent field of SciML, anchoring future development around critical pillars such as domain awareness, robustness, and interpretability. The SciML landscape has evolved profoundly over the past seven years. Considering these advancements, this workshop, hosted by the Center of Advanced Analytics and Predictive Sciences at the University of Augsburg, convenes researchers from diverse disciplines to re-evaluate the original priorities within the context of current technological frontiers. Through expert keynotes, technical presentations, and collaborative breakout sessions, participants will share practical insights and critically analyze current progress and emerging challenges within the field. Our primary objective is to assess the trajectory of the original PRDs and collaboratively shape the future research agenda for SciML. The insights generated during this two-day event will be synthesized into a comprehensive scientific article, targeting high-impact journals such as Nature Machine Intelligence or Neurocomputing.
We have synthesized the original six PRDs into four focused research directions, which participants will explore deeply during the breakout sessions.

title: Program
text:
Session types
The program combines invited keynotes, contributed presentations, and collaborative breakout sessions:

Keynotes have a 45-minute slot and set the stage for the discussion of the day.
Presentations are contributed talks of roughly 20 minutes each, thematically related to the breakout sessions they precede or follow.
Breakout sessions are the core of the workshop. Each session works on one of the four research directions in a small group, with the goal of critically assessing progress since the original priority research directions and identifying open challenges.
Presentation of breakout findings brings the groups back together to report their results to all participants.
Organizational and collaborative slots — session overview, session alignment, status sync, final result preparation, and the social event — are used to coordinate between the groups and to prepare the joint outcome of the workshop.

The findings collected during the breakout sessions form the basis of the joint scientific article that will be prepared after the workshop.
